Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key clinical findings and impressions:
  - Young female, ~3 days of dysuria (stinging on voiding), suprapubic crampy pain, malodorous urine and an episode of visible haematuria. No fever, no flank/back pain, no nausea/vomiting, no increased urinary frequency reported. Sexually active, never screened for STIs. Clinician interpreted presentation as most consistent with an acute uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection (cystitis) and planned empirical oral antibiotics and supportive measures.

- Relevant differentials from DDx consistent with transcript:
  - Acute uncomplicated cystitis — High likelihood. Classic cluster: dysuria, suprapubic pain, malodorous urine, haematuria; clinician diagnosis and plan consistent with this.  
  - Urethritis due to STI (Chlamydia/Gonorrhea) — Medium likelihood. Sexually active with no prior STI screening and dysuria without prominent discharge; DDx highlights need to consider/ test.  
  - Urolithiasis (lower urinary tract stone) — Low–Medium likelihood. Haematuria and lower abdominal pain could reflect a stone, but lack of severe colicky/flank radiation and systemic signs makes this less likely.

- Working diagnosis:
  - Acute uncomplicated cystitis (working diagnosis). Justification: symptomatic dysuria, suprapubic cramping, malodorous urine and visible haematuria in a young sexually active female; clinician also conveyed this diagnosis and initiated empirical antibiotic therapy.

- Considerations (additional plausible but uncertain options from DDx):
  - Urethritis due to sexually transmitted infection (Chlamydia/Gonorrhea) — consider NAAT testing and partner management.  
  - Urolithiasis — consider if haematuria persists or pain changes character.  
  - Ascending infection/pyelonephritis — low likelihood currently but monitor for fever, flank pain or systemic symptoms.

- Management documented in transcript:
  - Empirical oral antibiotic therapy discussed: either nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim; regimen described as one tablet twice daily for three days — specific drug selection and dose/route not documented.  
  - Advise increase oral fluids. Cranberry juice suggested as symptomatic aid.  
  - Advice to avoid sexual intercourse while symptomatic if possible; continue barrier contraception when sexually active.  
  - Safety-net: return or call if not improved by end of the week, or earlier if fever, back/flank pain, or feeling generally more unwell.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Acute uncomplicated cystitis (High): Young sexually active female with several days of dysuria, suprapubic cramping, malodorous urine and visible haematuria; clinician diagnosed and planned empirical antibiotics.
- Urethritis due to STI (Chlamydia/Gonorrhea) (Medium): Sexually active with no prior STI screening and dysuria without prominent vaginal discharge — NAAT testing should be considered.
- Urolithiasis (Low–Medium): Visible haematuria and lower abdominal pain could reflect a lower urinary tract stone, but lack of severe colicky or flank pain and systemic signs makes this less likely.
